description:
Second year physics student at Imperial, competing in person at the London event, 14 to 15 Nov. Doing the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge: pick a landing site near the lunar south pole and a date, and the tool works out from NASA ephemerides and terrain data when it is in sunlight and can see Earth. I’ll take the geometry and data side.

Looking for two people: one for the frontend (map, date slider, moving shadows), one for video, page and pitch. Two full days, no space background needed.
summary: Missions to the Moon's south pole live or die on two things: sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communication. Both depend on the exact landing spot and date, because the Sun and Earth sit within a few degrees of the horizon and any ridge can block them. Our tool lets a mission planner pick a landing point, a date, a mission length and a mast height, and see straight away where the Sun and Earth are against the real terrain horizon, how much sunlight and Earth contact the mission gets, how long the longest darkness lasts, and whether the mission meets its requirements. It compares scenarios side by side and shows every landing date in the year that works. The numbers are computed from NASA laser altimeter terrain and NASA ephemeris data, and checked against JPL Horizons and published illumination studies.
details:
We built a tool for working out where and when you can land at the Moon's south pole without your lander dying.

The problem: at the south pole the Sun and the Earth both sit right on the horizon. One ridge in the wrong place and you lose your solar power, or your radio link, or both. And it changes with the date. So "is this a good landing site" depends on exactly where and exactly when.

What you do with it

You pick a landing point, a date, how long the mission lasts and how tall your mast is. Then you get:

- a 360 degree view of the real horizon from that spot, with the Sun and Earth where they would be at that hour. Press play and you watch the Sun crawl along the horizon and disappear behind the terrain

- an hour by hour timeline of sunlight and Earth contact

- the numbers that matter: how much sunlight, how much Earth contact, the longest stretch of darkness, the longest comms gap, time until the next sunset

- a pass or fail verdict against requirements you set yourself (how long your lander survives in the dark, how much Earth contact you need, max slope and so on)

- up to four scenarios side by side, so you can compare a 1 m mast against a 5 m mast, or this month against next month

- a calendar of every landing date in 2027 showing which ones work

- a map of the ten landing points from above

One thing we like: the whole page goes dark when the Sun is behind the terrain at the hour you are looking at. You notice straight away when your site loses power.

How it works

All the hard maths is done beforehand in Python and saved into one data file. The website just reads it, which is why it is instant.

- Sun and Earth positions come from NASA's SPICE kernels, every hour for a year, for each landing point

- for the horizon we look in 720 directions from each point and find the highest bit of terrain in each one, using NASA LOLA laser altimeter maps: 5 m resolution nearby, then the 5 m south pole mosaic, then a 240 m map out to about 300 km

- then for every hour we work out how much of the Sun's disc and the Earth's disc is above that horizon, for a 1 m mast and a 5 m mast

- ground temperature comes from a simple radiative balance model

We cover ten points across four areas: Connecting ridge, Shackleton rim, de Gerlache rim and Malapert massif.

Does it give the right answers

We checked, because a pretty tool with wrong numbers is useless.

- our Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons to 0.00003 degrees

- our sunlight numbers for Connecting ridge sit inside the range published by Barker et al. (2021) for the same place, and with a 5 m mast we are within half a percentage point of their best value

- our thermal model gives 386 K at the equator at noon. Diviner measured 387 to 390 K

- the full table and plots are in the repo under docs/validation

Things we found out along the way

- far away mountains matter more than we expected. Malapert massif is about 130 km from Connecting ridge and it still blocks the Earth. Leaving out distant terrain overstates Earth contact there by up to 11.5 percentage points

- a taller mast fixes power but does nothing for comms at that site. Going from 1 m to 5 m takes sunlight from 81% to 92% over 2027. Earth contact stays at 51%

- no site is best at everything. Connecting ridge gets the most Sun. Malapert gets the most Earth contact (around 80%) and the least Sun

- a few hundred metres changes a lot. At one point on Shackleton rim the longest darkness in 2027 is 16.6 days with a 1 m mast and 2.9 days with a 5 m mast

Who it is for

Mission planners who need a fast answer when a launch date slips or the hardware changes. Also students and anyone curious about why landing at the south pole is so hard, since you can see the reason on screen.

What it does not do

- you cannot type in your own coordinates, because the horizons are worked out in advance

- the lander temperature settings in the verdict are example values

- ground temperature is on the cold side when the Sun is only grazing the surface

What we used

Python (numpy, rasterio, pyproj, spiceypy, astroquery, matplotlib) for the calculations. React and Vite for the website. GitHub Pages to host it. We used AI tools to help write and check code and docs, and logged every use in docs/ai_use.md.

Code: https://github.com/HarukiMatsu/hayabusa-lunar-navigator
